summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex medical history including end-stage renal disease, functioning pancreatic transplants, mechanical mitral valve, and peripheral vascular disease was admitted with fever and left lower extremity cellulitis, three days after noticing worsening redness and pain. She had a recent popliteal stent placement for a non-healing ulcer. On admission, she had a supratherapeutic INR of 10.1, which was corrected with vitamin K, and was started on a heparin drip. Blood cultures from the outside hospital grew Corynebacterium striatum, prompting treatment with IV vancomycin and levofloxacin. Imaging showed severe left-sided peripheral arterial disease with a necrotic left toe, and vascular surgery recommended amputation to prevent infection spread. The patient declined immediate surgery, opting to decide after discharge. Her infection improved clinically and laboratory markers trended favorably. She was discharged to extended care on a heparin drip, warfarin, IV vancomycin, and oral levofloxacin, with plans to follow up with her podiatrist regarding amputation.
